title: India chairs BRICS in 2026: the trade union track
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Where the BRICS Trade Union Forum fits.
body:
BRICS began as a grouping of Brazil, Russia, India and China, and South Africa joined in 2010. The group has since grown beyond its original five members, and India holds the **chair of BRICS in 2026**. Most readers associate BRICS with trade, finance and summit photographs. Less well known is that the grouping also has a labour track, in which ministers, officials and trade union leaders meet to discuss jobs, social protection and the future of work. Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh (BMS) has a direct role in that track this year. This post explains how the labour track is organised, where the trade union forum fits, what BMS was preparing to do as host, and why the discussions matter to ordinary workers. An update at the end records what happened in July.

## How the labour track is organised

BRICS decisions are taken by member governments, but the group has built a series of working channels around the leaders' summit. Labour sits in two of them.

- The **Labour and Employment Working Group**, where officials prepare the ground, and the **Labour and Employment Ministers' Meeting**, where the ministers of member countries adopt a declaration. In 2026 the ministers' meeting was scheduled in Hyderabad.
- The **BRICS Trade Union Forum (TUF)**, which brings together the national trade union centres of the member countries. It meets before or around the summit season and adopts a declaration addressed to the leaders and the ministers. In 2026 a delegation of the forum was to present its views at the ministers' meeting.

The forum is not a decision-making body, and its declaration does not bind any government. Its value lies in access. It lets workers' organisations put their priorities to ministers in the same city and in the same week, before the final texts are settled.

## Who takes part from India

India's trade union centres take part in the BRICS Trade Union Forum, and BMS is among them. BMS also sits on the workers' side of India's delegation to the International Labour Organization (ILO), where similar questions, such as platform work and social protection, are discussed. As chair of BRICS in 2026, India was to host the forum, and BMS was to host the **15th BRICS Trade Union Forum Summit**. This blog reports on the summit in a later post.

## Why these meetings matter

The member countries of BRICS include some of the largest labour markets in the world, with a very large share of the world's working people. The principles they agree on carry weight beyond their borders, because other developing countries watch what the group says. Several subjects on the labour agenda are of direct concern to workers.

- **Social protection.** Many workers in BRICS countries work in the informal economy, with no pension, no health cover and no insurance against accident. Extending protection to them, and making it portable from one employer or place to another, is the central issue.
- **Migration.** Workers move within countries and across borders, and benefits earned in one place are often lost in the next.
- **Technology.** Artificial intelligence, automation and digital platforms are changing the nature of jobs, and the question is whether technology will assist workers or replace them.
- **Women's work.** Female labour force participation and equal pay are problems in every member country.
- **Skills and just transition.** Workers in industries that are changing need retraining and a path to new work.

## The BMS note

BMS has said at international forums that a global economic order must be **worker-centric**, in line with its slogan, *Workers unite the world.* Speaking at the ILO in Geneva on 9 June 2026, its representative stressed that quality jobs with fair wages, social protection, safety and skills matter as much as the bare creation of employment, that technology should assist people rather than replace them, and that safe migration, portable benefits and equal treatment are shared responsibilities of governments, employers and trade unions. He also cited a recognition by the International Social Security Association of India's social security coverage, which he put at 64 per cent of the workforce, and the point he drew was that coverage should be extended further and made real. The same concerns are what BMS carries into the BRICS forum.

## Update: what happened in Hyderabad

The ministers' meeting was held in Hyderabad on 15 and 16 July 2026. According to the ILO, which welcomed the outcome, the ministers set four priorities: expanding social security and formal work; women's participation in the workforce; employability and skills; and the use of digital technology to protect all workers, including gig and platform workers, in a rights-based and well-governed way. They also adopted **BRICS CONNECT**, a cooperation network for capacity building, employability, skills and technology. The ILO noted a feasibility study on an international occupational classification, undertaken with India and Brazil, and its own estimate that a universal care policy package could create about 165 million jobs across BRICS countries by 2030.

The **15th BRICS Trade Union Forum Summit** ran in Hyderabad from 14 to 16 July 2026, hosted by BMS. According to a report, 53 delegates from national trade union centres of 13 member and partner countries took part, together with more than 60 other participants including union leaders, human-resource experts, industry representatives and academics, and the Governor of Telangana gave the closing address. The summit unanimously adopted the **Hyderabad Declaration**. It calls on governments to expand universal, adequate and sustainable social protection that includes unorganised, self-employed, migrant, platform, agricultural and non-standard workers; it sets four priorities that mirror the ministers' list, namely women and work, universal social security with cross-border portability, continuous skills development and human-centred technology; it asks for a permanent BRICS mechanism for engaging trade unions; it urges member countries to align national laws quickly to guarantee collective bargaining and social protection for platform workers; and it welcomes the ILO's 2026 convention on decent work in the platform economy. A delegation led by the forum's chairman presented the workers' views at the ministers' meeting.

## What remains to be done

A declaration is a promise, and the test is what follows. For the labour track, three things deserve watching. One is whether the permanent mechanism for trade union engagement is actually created, so that dialogue does not depend on who holds the chair in a given year. Another is how the commitments on social protection translate into national schemes, with funding and a way for informal workers to enrol. The third is whether BRICS CONNECT delivers practical results, such as shared skills data that help a worker find training or a job across borders.

## In closing

International meetings can seem remote from the daily life of a worker on a shop floor, a delivery rider or a farm labourer. They are not. The standards and promises made there become the reference points that unions use in their own country when they ask for a scheme, a law or a rule. That is why BMS prepares for these meetings as seriously as it does for a local negotiation.
